content: The 2015 Global Survey on Health Technology Assessment (HTA) by National Authorities, conducted by the World Health Organization (WHO), aimed to evaluate the use and implementation of HTA processes globally. The findings and methodologies of this survey are detailed in the report, which was developed under the direction of Marie-Paule Kieny, WHO Assistant Director-General for Health Systems and Innovation. The survey was coordinated by Adriana Velazquez, with guidance from Gilles Forte and Kees de Joncheere of the WHO Department of Essential Medicines and Health Products (EMP). The survey was designed to assess the utilization of HTA in public sector decision-making, the scope of HTA and availability of guidelines, institutional capacity and human resources supporting HTA, governance of HTA processes, and requirements for strengthening HTA capacity. It was distributed to all WHO Member States through their Permanent Missions in Geneva, with a request to nominate a national HTA focal point within their Ministry of Health. The questionnaire was available in six official UN languages: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian, and Spanish. The survey revealed that most countries reported having a formal process for systematically compiling, analyzing, and synthesizing relevant information and scientific evidence to support healthcare policy decision-making. However, one-third of the responding countries did not explicitly refer to this process as HTA. Highand upper-middle-income countries, particularly in the European (EUR) and American (AMR) regions, were more likely to have formal HTA processes. In contrast, low-income countries often lacked well-defined processes, relying instead on informal evidence consideration. The primary purposes of HTA varied by income level. Low-income countries and 85% of middle-income countries used HTA primarily for planning and budgeting. High-income countries were more likely to use HTA for determining reimbursement policies or deciding on benefit package inclusions. In the European region, 80% of countries used HTA findings for reimbursement decisions, compared to 28%-62% in other regions. The scope of HTA focused predominantly on safety, clinical effectiveness, and economic and budgetary impact. Other considerations, such as acceptability to healthcare providers and patients, equity issues, ethical concerns, and feasibility, were less frequently addressed. Most countries (53%-92%) consistently considered safety across all types of health technologies or interventions. Clinical effectiveness was also deemed important, with 65%-85% of respondents highlighting it as a key aspect of HTA. Guidelines for HTA were most commonly available for medicines (82% of countries) and vaccines (67%). However, fewer countries reported having guidelines for other types of health technologies, such as surgical interventions or service delivery models. Institutional capacity and human resources supporting HTA were more robust in high-income countries compared to low-income countries. Most countries reported having a national entity with more than six staff members dedicated to producing HTA reports for the Ministry of Health. These staff members were typically public health and clinical science professionals. In the Americas (AMR) and Europe (EUR), 81%-83% of countries reported having such entities, compared to 33%-77% in other regions. Requests for HTA reports were primarily made by Ministries of Health or public insurance bodies. In the 12 months preceding the survey, 45% of respondents reported that HTAs were always or almost always requested by these entities, while 25% reported similar requests from reimbursement bodies. The survey findings underscore the importance of HTA in informing healthcare policy and decision-making, particularly in the context of universal health coverage. However, the report also highlights disparities in HTA capacity and utilization across regions and income levels, emphasizing the need for targeted efforts to strengthen HTA systems globally.
